Vanessa: Well, that really was an epic experience. Michelle, I learned so many cool bits of information, which I think will definitely stick with me for a long time.
Michelle: You're welcome, Vanessa. Since you liked stargazing, I'll take you to other amazing places. If you like, we can check out another place next week.
Vanessa: That would be fantastic! Let me check my schedule first, I might be busy next week. I might have to decline.
Michelle: Okay. If you come, I'll bring my kids, who I think will enjoy this experience very much. It should be fun stargazing with a bigger group.

Vanessa: That sounds like fun! Oh. I'm sorry Michelle, but next week it looks like the restaurant staff and I have a big meeting.
Michelle: Oh it's no problem. It might be raining next week anyways. So, are you reconsidering the Mars exploration idea?
Vanessa: Of course not! I should be able to find tons of research material on it. You should also call your friend who you think can help us. He must know a lot about Mars.
Michelle: That sounds like a great plan! He should be available to meet next week. Why don't you come as well? If you agree to come, I'll convince him to join us on this project.

Vanessa: Well, I have to see. It really depends on the head chef, who is usually bent on having me stay late. If he doesn't allow me to come, I obviously can't make it. Anyway, if he won't let me leave early, I can't.
Michelle: Well, please try. Tell him if he is willing to let you off the hook, we'll make room for him to come to Mars with us!
Vanessa: If you don't mind, I would rather not ask him to come. He won't be so easily enticed. Besides, I will not spend another disastrous social evening with him.
Michelle: We will have fun no matter what happens.

You can use relative clauses to modify a noun. This can be both the subject and object of the sentence.

Depending on the noun you are referring to, you may have to create a defining relative clause or a non-defining relative clause. These may also be called restrictive and non-restrictive adjective clauses, respectively.

A defining relative clause is necessary to explain which noun you are talking about.
A non-defining relative clause is extra, non-essential information about the noun. You need to use commas with this clause.
Relative pronouns are also important in relative clauses.

That is interchangeable for both people and things, but it is more commonly used to refer to things. Who is only used for people.

In relative clauses modifying an object where a preposition is needed with a verb, if the preposition is placed before the relative pronoun, only whom or which can be used. Do not use that in this instance.
You should also call your friend who you think can help us.

It really depends on the head chef, who is usually bent on having me stay late.
The head chef, who is my boss, insists that I stay late at work.
Modal Verbs for Speculating about the Present
You can speculate about present situations using modal verbs. These verbs convey a special meaning and are followed by the base form of the verb.
Each of the following words carries a different meaning. You need to choose the correct one based on what you want to say.

Will is also used with if to show polite requests, refusals and disapproval. Using will in the if-clause for these reasons is different from expressing future possibility. Remember, an if-clause is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone. It must be added to a dependent clause to make a complete sentence.
